title: Children's digital access is near-universal, while platform activity and safety risks make protection, empowerment, and child voice institutional problems
source_unit: OECD How's Life for Children in the Digital Age?, cross-national synthesis of PISA, HBSC, and PIRLS data
geography: OECD countries, with indicators using the report's specified international country subsets and survey years

observations.period: 2021-2022 international data summarized in OECD 2025 report

denominator.unit: OECD-country comparison frame; individual indicators use their own survey country subsets

fifteen_year_old_home_device_access.unit: percent of 15-year-olds with access to a desktop computer, laptop, or tablet at home

fifteen_year_old_smartphone_internet_acc.unit: percent of 15-year-olds with a smartphone and Internet connection

fifteen_year_old_thirty_plus_device_hour.unit: at least half of 15-year-olds in most OECD countries spending 30 or more hours per week on digital devices

fifteen_year_old_sixty_plus_online_range.unit: percent of 15-year-olds spending 60 or more hours online, ranging from Japan to Latvia

ten_year_old_own_smartphone.unit: approximate OECD average percent of 10-year-olds owning a smartphone

observations.method: OECD compiles cross-national indicators from PISA 2022, Health Behaviour in School-aged Children 2021-22, and PIRLS 2021 to describe device access, time, activities, and differences by age, gender, socio-economic status, and family context.
observations.uncertainty: Country coverage and question wording vary by indicator, and access is not equivalent to quality, safety, learning, or well-being. Reported averages conceal large country and household differences and do not establish that device time causes a particular outcome.
observations.subgroup: Children and adolescents, especially 10-year-olds and 15-year-olds; comparisons include gender, socio-economic status, migrant background, and family structure where reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-universal access can expand learning, information, play, and connection. High device time can be productive or social; the report stresses activity type, service design, and offline context rather than screen time alone.

observations.period: 2017-18 to 2021-22 HBSC comparison and 2022 OECD digital-wellbeing synthesis

denominator.unit: adolescents aged 11, 13, and 15 across OECD comparison countries; country and age coverage follows HBSC reporting

problematic_social_media_use.unit: approximately percent of adolescents reporting problematic social-media use in 2021-22, up from less than 7% in 2017-18

problematic_use_girls.unit: percent of girls reporting problematic social-media use

problematic_use_boys.unit: percent of boys reporting problematic social-media use

problematic_use_migrant_background.unit: percent of adolescents with a migrant background reporting problematic social-media use, compared with 10% among native-born adolescents

three_plus_hours_social_media_weekday.unit: percent of 15-year-olds spending at least three hours on social media on a typical weekday

observations.method: OECD interprets HBSC repeated cross-sectional indicators alongside evidence on digital activity type, passive versus active engagement, platform design, social comparison, cyberbullying, family context, and offline vulnerabilities.
observations.uncertainty: Problematic-use measures are self-reported and do not diagnose addiction, depression, anxiety, or causal harm. The time-series comparison is not a single longitudinal cohort, and the report emphasizes that population-average effects can be modest while risks remain concentrated in vulnerable groups.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents by gender, age, migration background, socio-economic status, family structure, and patterns of social-media use.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher reported exposure among girls or migrant-background adolescents may reflect different use, disclosure, measurement, or social context rather than uniformly greater harm. Regulation, parental guidance, education, and platform design can change the risk environment.

related_sources.claim: OECD summarizes device access, time, activities, problematic use, and its rights-based policy framing.
OECD separately examines age-assurance practices as a platform and institutional-control route.

boundary: This record adds a child digital-access, activity, exposure, and institutional-protection route distinct from the UNICEF abuse/reporting record and the broader adult social-connection and internet-wellbeing records. It does not diagnose children, estimate platform causality, or treat device time as a standalone harm measure.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: OECD publication page, executive summary, introduction/main-findings chapter, and digital-activities chapter retrieved; device access, time, activity, problematic-use, subgroup, and uncertainty statements cross-checked against official OECD materials.
